summary: Lists DHCP option codes that were assigned to proposed options which were never used, and directs IANA to make them available for assignment to other options. It also lists several codes not currently documented in an RFC. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A coat rack has hooks that nobody uses. This document says which hooks are empty, so they can be given to new coats instead of staying wasted.

questions: which dhcp option codes are free
which dhcp option codes are unused
what dhcp option codes were reclaimed
why were dhcp option codes returned to iana
subtitle: A cleanup list of DHCP option codes that were never used and can be reassigned.

tldr.problem: Several DHCP option codes were assigned to proposed options that were never used, leaving them locked up in the IANA list.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the unused codes with their history, directs IANA to make them available for new options, and names other undocumented codes that must be kept.
tldr.outcome: IANA has returned the listed codes, which may be reassigned following RFC 2939. The RFC has been updated by RFC 8910.

today: RFC 3679 is an Informational RFC that has been updated by RFC 8910. It records an IANA cleanup of DHCP option codes.

sections.title: Why Reclaim Option Codes
sections.content:
Before RFC 2489 (updated by RFC 2939), several DHCP option codes were assigned to proposed options that were subsequently never used. This document lists those codes from the IANA list of BOOTP and DHCP option codes, along with any known documentation and contact information.

It has two lists. Section 2 holds the codes to be returned to IANA for reassignment. Section 3 holds codes that are not documented in an RFC but should not be reassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: Some hooks on the coat rack were reserved for coats that never came. This memo tidies up the list so unused hooks can be reused.

sections.title: Codes To Be Reassigned
sections.content:
Twelve groups of codes are listed with the reason each can be recovered. Examples: code 80 (Service Location Protocol Naming Authority), codes 83 and 84 (Relay Agent Options, from an early draft of RFC 3046 and not defined in the published RFC), code 88 (IEEE 1003.1 POSIX Timezone), code 89 (FQDNs in DHCP Options), and code 96 (IPv6 Transition).

Others are 91 (VINES TCP/IP Server), 92 (Server Selection), 100 (Printer Name), 101 (Multicast Assignment through DHCP), 108 (Swap Path) and 110 (IPX Compatibility). Code 115 (Failover) came from early revisions of the DHCP Failover Protocol, whose current version does not use a DHCP option.

The usual reasons are that the option was never published as a standard or Internet-Draft, or was not in general use. Where a contact agreed, the RFC notes it.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the empty hooks. Some were meant for coats that were never made, so they can be handed out again.

sections.title: Codes To Keep
sections.content:
Some undocumented codes stay on the IANA list while the DHC working group decides what to do. Codes 93 (Client System), 94 (Client NDI) and 97 (UUID/GUID Client Identifier) are used in the PXE Specification, Version 2.1, and are in widespread use by PXE devices, yet have no published RFC.

Apple devices use 95 (LDAP Servers), 112 and 113 (Netinfo Address and Tag) and 114 (URL), also never published in an RFC. Codes 126 and 127 are identified for Option Code Extensions and return to IANA if not used for that. The DHC working group will try to have the PXE and Apple options published.

Section 4 adds that codes 99, 102 to 107, 109 and 111 were already returned for reassignment.
sections.plainLanguage: A few hooks look empty but are really in use, so they stay reserved until the grown-ups decide what to do with them.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has returned the codes listed in Section 2 to the available list. They may be reassigned to new DHCP options according to the procedures in RFC 2939. IANA is asked to reassign them only after the list of codes never assigned or previously returned has been exhausted.

The RFC says it has no known security implications, as none of the reclaimed options are known to be in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The person who keeps the hook list has freed up the unused hooks, but will hand out brand-new ones first.

references.text: Patrick, M., "DHCP Relay Agent Information Option", RFC 3046, January 2001.
Droms, R., "Procedures and IANA Guidelines for Definition of New DHCP Options and Message Types", BCP 43, RFC 2939, September 2000.
